passages.title: The jinn overhear a wondrous Qur'an
passages.tafsir:
Surah al-Jinn opens not with Allah addressing mankind directly, but with an instruction to the Prophet ﷺ to *report* something. Ibn Kathir states the purpose plainly: Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to inform his people that the jinn listened to the Qur'an, believed in it, affirmed its truthfulness and adhered to it.

Ayat 1 and 2 are the opening of that report — the moment of listening, and the declaration of faith that came out of it. They move as one unit: an unseen creation hears the Qur'an, calls it wondrous, finds that it guides, believes, and pledges never to join anything with its Lord. That last pledge is *tawhid* — holding Allah to be one, with no partner beside Him.

## "Say: it has been revealed to me"

Look at how ayah 1 begins. Not "you heard them" or "you saw them", but **قُلْ أُوحِيَ إِلَيَّ** — *qul uhiya ilayya*, "Say: it has been revealed to me." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out what this wording implies: it shows that the Prophet ﷺ did not see the group of jinn who heard him recite the Qur'an. Allah informed him by the revelation of Surah al-Jinn.

Maʿārif returns to the point later and puts it beyond doubt: the Prophet ﷺ was not even aware of the jinn's coming to him and listening to the Qur'an that is mentioned in this surah; he learnt about it only later, through revelation.

So the whole passage reaches us at one remove. The jinn spoke to their own people; Allah told His Messenger ﷺ; the Messenger ﷺ was told to tell us. The recitation went out and was received by listeners the reciter could not see.

**"A group" — نَفَرٌ مِّنَ الْجِنِّ.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Arabic word *nafar* is used for a group of three to ten. The jinn referred to here are said to be a group of nine, from a place called Nasibin. Not a nation, not a crowd — a handful, out on an errand.

**"Listened" — اسْتَمَعَ.** In the account Maʿārif relays, when this group of jinn heard the Qur'an "they listened to it very attentively." That attentiveness is the hinge of the whole episode.

## What the jinn actually are

Because this surah is built on their testimony, it helps to know who is testifying. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Tafsir Mazhari, gives a compact description.

The jinn are one of the Divine creatures. They have body and soul. Like human beings they have intellect and senses, but they are hidden from human eyes — and that is precisely why they carry this name, since the word *jinn* literally means "hidden" or "invisible". Like human beings they are created from the four primal elements — dust, water, air and fire — but the element of fire predominates in them, whereas in man the element of dust predominates. They are males and females; they marry and they procreate. Apparently, says Mazhari, the word *shaitan* (plural *shayatin*) refers to the arrogant mischief-making jinn. And the existence of jinn and angels is established by conclusive and incontestable evidence in the Qur'an and Sunnah — its denial or rejection amounts to disbelieving the Qur'an.

Two things follow. First, the jinn are not folkloric decoration; they are creatures with intellect, which is why their reasoning in these ayat is worth recording. Second, on Mazhari's description "jinn" is not a synonym for "devil" — *shaitan* names the arrogant mischief-makers among them, and the ones in this passage are precisely those who chose otherwise.

## Why they were out searching

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the background as a set of facts to know before reading the surah. The first is this: before the advent of the Prophet ﷺ, the devils used to go up to the heavens and eavesdrop on the conversations of the angels. After his advent, they were pelted with a piercing flame if they attempted to go up and eavesdrop. Surah al-Ahqaf mentions a group of jinn going to the Prophet ﷺ to investigate the reason for this new phenomenon.

The fullest account comes from Sayyidna Ibn 'Abbas, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports it as recorded in Sahih of Bukhari, of Muslim, and in Tirmidhi and other collections. Its opening point is a negative one, and it matters: Allah's Messenger ﷺ did not by deliberate design make the jinn listen to the Qur'an, nor did he see them.

What happened was this. The Prophet ﷺ, with his Companions, was going to the marketplace of 'Ukaz. This took place at the time when the devils were barred from going to the skies and eavesdropping by being pelted with piercing flames. Realising they were no longer free to eavesdrop, the jinn discussed among themselves that this could not be coincidental — there must be a genuine reason for it. So they divided themselves into groups, and each group went in a different direction to investigate the cause.

One of those groups arrived at a place called Nakhlah in Tihamah, where Hijaz is situated. At that juncture the Prophet ﷺ was leading the Sahabah — his Companions — in the Fajr *salah*, the dawn prayer, and the jinn had the opportunity to hear the Qur'an. They listened very attentively, and concluded on oath that it was the Qur'an that had prevented them from eavesdropping in the heavens. Then they returned to their fellow jinn and recounted to them the entire episode.

That last sentence is what ayah 1 is quoting. **فَقَالُوا** — "and they said" — is their report to their own kind. They had gone out looking for the reason the sky had closed against them, and what they found was recitation.

## The road back from Ta'if

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also relays, on the authority of Mazhari, the setting most commentators give for the Nakhlah incident — and it is one of the heaviest moments in the Prophet's ﷺ life.

After the death of Abu Talib the Prophet ﷺ felt lonely, having no friend or supporter in Makkah. So he undertook a journey to Ta'if, where he approached Banu Thaqif for assistance against the hostility and persecution of his people. According to Muhammad Ibn Ishaq's narration he approached three brothers of Banu Thaqif, recognised as the leaders and honourable members of the tribe — 'Umair's sons, named 'Abd Yalil, Sa'ud and Habib. He invited them to the call of Islam, mentioned his people's hostility and persecution, and asked for help. They responded very harshly and did not speak to him about anything.

Seeing the door closed, he asked one small thing: if they did not wish to help him, they should at least keep his arrival and his request confidential and not tell his people — because if they came to know of it, they would persecute him even more harshly. The oppressors did not concede to this either. On the contrary, they let loose on him foolish hooligans, slaves and hoodlums, to revile him and make violent noises in public places against him; and when the noise began, more hoodlums and violent young men joined in. To save himself from this, the Prophet ﷺ took refuge in a vineyard belonging to two brothers, 'Utbah and Shaibah, who were themselves in the vineyard at the time and watched both him and how violently the foolish people had behaved towards him.

When he felt a bit settled in the vineyard, he prayed to Allah. Maʿārif notes that the wordings of this supplication are unusual and that on no other occasion are such wordings recorded. Maʿārif gives the wording as condensed from Mazhari, and in its rendering it runs:

*"O Allah, I complain to you the weakness of my strength and the shortage of my options, and lack of respect for me in the sight of people. You are the Most Merciful of all, and You are the Cherisher and Sustainer of the weaklings. You are my Cherisher. To whom are You handing me over? — to a stranger who would attack me? Or to an enemy whom You have given control over me…? If You are not angry with me, I do not care."*

He goes on to seek refuge in the light of Allah's blessed Being, which dispels all darkness and by which the affairs of this world and the next are set right, and closes with the acknowledgement that there is neither strength nor power except through Him.

Watching this, Rabi'ah's sons 'Utbah and Shaibah felt compassion for him in their hearts. They called a Christian slave of theirs, 'Addas by name, and had him bring a bunch of grapes on a plate. The Prophet ﷺ recited *bismillah* — "In the name of Allah" — and stretched his hand towards it. 'Addas said: By Allah, this speech is not used by the inhabitants of this city. Asked where he was from and what his religion was, he replied that he was a Christian and hailed from Nineveh. The Prophet ﷺ told him that this meant he was from the village of Yunus ibn Matta (peace be upon him). 'Addas asked what he knew of Yunus ibn Matta. He replied: "He was my brother. He was Allah's Prophet. I too am Allah's Prophet." At this 'Addas fell to his feet and kissed his blessed head, his hands and his legs — and when he returned to his masters and they asked him about it, he said that at that time there was no person better than he on the face of the earth, for he had taught him something which none other than a Prophet can teach.

When the Prophet ﷺ was completely despaired of Thaqif's assistance, he returned from Ta'if towards Makkah. On the way back he halted at Nakhlah, and towards the latter part of the night he performed *salat-ut-tahajjud* — the voluntary prayer offered in the depth of the night. The delegation of jinn of Nasibin of Yemen had also gone there. They heard the Qur'an and embraced the faith, and went back to their people and recounted the whole incident — which is what these ayat record.

**On the two accounts.** As Maʿārif relays them, the reports differ in their surrounding detail: the narration from Ibn 'Abbas places the incident on a journey towards 'Ukaz, with the Prophet ﷺ leading Fajr; the account from Mazhari places it on the return from Ta'if, during tahajjud. Both converge on Nakhlah, on the jinn of Nasibin, and above all on the point ayah 1 itself insists upon — that the Prophet ﷺ knew nothing of it until revelation came.

And there is something here to sit with. On the setting most commentators give, this was a moment of great isolation: no Abu Talib left in Makkah, and the leaders of Thaqif answering so harshly that they would not speak to him about anything. The tribal chiefs he had come to, who could see him and hear him plainly, would not give him a word. Unseen, a different creation entirely was listening — and believing.

## The two words the jinn chose

**قُرْآنًا عَجَبًا.** Ibn Kathir renders it "a wonderful Recitation"; Maʿārif, "an amazing Recital". Notice what they reached for first. Not "we heard a law", not "we heard a warning" — the first thing in their report is wonder.

**يَهْدِي إِلَى الرُّشْدِ — "It guides to the right path."** Ayah 2 gives the second thing they noticed, and it is the thing wonder alone could never supply. Ibn Kathir glosses the phrase: "meaning, to what is correct and success." His gloss names two things, not one — being correct, and arriving at success. They did not merely find the Qur'an impressive; they found that it *took them somewhere*.

The movement across these two ayat is worth tracing as a whole, because it is the anatomy of a sound conversion: they listened very attentively → they called it a wonderful Recitation → they saw that it guides to the right path → they believed in it → they pledged never to join anything with their Lord.

## "And we have believed therein, and we shall never join anything with our Lord"

**فَآمَنَّا بِهِ** — "and we have believed therein." In their own report, hearing the guidance and believing in it sit inside a single breath. Ibn Kathir notes that the position they took here is similar to what Allah said elsewhere: *"And when We sent towards you a group of the Jinns listening to the Qur'an"* (46:29).

**وَلَن نُّشْرِكَ بِرَبِّنَا أَحَدًا** — "and we shall never join anything with our Lord." This is a renunciation of *shirk*: associating anything or anyone with Allah in what belongs to Him alone.

Two things are worth pausing over. First, the pledge is about the future, not merely the past — it is not only *we were wrong*, but *we shall never*. Second, the first fruit of their faith, as they themselves report it, was not a ritual but a renunciation. Guidance showed itself by what it made them refuse.

There is a quiet irony in this, given the background Maʿārif supplies. He records as a preliminary fact that in the Days of Ignorance, travellers halting in a jungle or valley would say: *"I seek refuge in the leader of this valley from the foolish mischief-makers of his nation"* — believing that the leader of the valley, a jinn, would protect them. Human beings were seeking refuge in jinn. And here are jinn declaring that they will never join anything with their Lord.

## A note: this is not the "Night of the Jinn"

Readers often merge two separate events, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to keep them apart. According to the hadith narratives that recount the incident of the "Night of Jinn", Sayyidna 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud was with the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ met the jinn in a valley near Makkah for the specific purpose of inviting them to the call of Islam and making them hear the Qur'an *by deliberate design*. Apparently that incident occurred after the one mentioned in Surah al-Jinn. The event of this surah was neither planned nor witnessed by him; he learnt of it only afterwards through revelation, and it happened at Nakhlah on his way back from Ta'if. 'Allamah Khafaji has said that reliable ahadith confirm the jinn delegations met the Prophet ﷺ six times — so there is no contradiction between the two versions; they are two separate incidents.

Maʿārif also relates a striking postscript from Ibn Jauzi's *Sifat-us-Safwah*, reported through his own chain of authorities from Sahl ibn 'Abdullah: that Sahl once saw an old jinn performing *salah* in the direction of the Ka'bah, wearing a woollen cloak that looked beautiful on him. When Sahl greeted him and he replied, the jinn said that the cloak had been on his body for seven hundred years, that he had met the Prophet 'Isa (peace be upon him) in it and met the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the same cloak — and that he was among those jinn about whom Surah al-Jinn was revealed.

## Living it

**Recitation reaches further than the reciter can see.** Maʿārif's plainest point on ayah 1 is that the Prophet ﷺ did not see the jinn who heard him, and was not even aware of the incident until revelation came. A whole surah came out of a recitation whose audience the reciter did not know he had.

**Listen the way they listened.** They listened very attentively — and were changed. The leaders of Thaqif, in the same account, heard the invitation directly from the Prophet ﷺ and responded so harshly that they would not speak to him about anything. The difference was not access; it was attention.

**Judge guidance by what it makes you give up.** Their test of the Qur'an in ayah 2 was that it guides to the right path — and the proof they offered was not an emotion but a commitment: *we shall never join anything with our Lord.* Ask of anything that moves you spiritually what it has actually made you renounce.

**And keep the Ta'if pairing in view.** On the setting most commentators give, on the journey home from the door that had closed hardest, an entirely different creation was being brought to faith by his recitation — and he did not know it until Allah told him. Allah's answer to a servant's need does not have to arrive through the door the servant is watching.

passages.title: The lies about Allah the jinn now disown
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are still the jinn speaking — the report of what that listening group said after the Qur'an reached their ears. Having declared their faith and their refusal of *shirk* — associating anything with Allah as a partner — in ayat 1–2, they now turn and look back at what they used to believe, naming the lie about Allah, naming who first spoke it, and confessing how they came to swallow it.

**What holds them together.** Each ayah opens with the same little hinge — *wa annahu*, *wa annā*, *wa annahum*, "and that…" — so the passage reads like a sworn statement given item by item: *and that* our Lord has no consort or child (ayah 3); *and that* the fool among us used to say outrageous things about Him (ayah 4); *and that* we assumed no one would dare lie about Allah (ayah 5); *and that* men used to seek refuge with jinn (ayah 6); *and that* they assumed, as you assumed, that Allah would send no one (ayah 7). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that commentators discussed the grammar of this repeated *wa annahu* at length, but adds that the technical debate is of little interest to the general reader. What matters is the shape: a creed affirmed, then an autopsy of the falsehood they have just walked out of.

## Ayah 3: "Exalted is the *jadd* of our Lord"

The first thing these new believers say about Allah is a word of sheer magnification: **تَعَالَىٰ جَدُّ رَبِّنَا** — *taʿālā jaddu rabbinā*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *jadd* as "majesty" or "glory" when used of Allah. Ibn Kathir gathers what the early authorities said about it, and the range is worth seeing:

- **Ibn ʿAbbas** (reported by ʿAli bin Abi Talhah): "This means, His actions, His commands and His power."
- **Ibn ʿAbbas** (reported by Ad-Dahhak): "Allah's *Jadd* is His blessings, His power and His favor upon His creation."
- **Mujahid and ʿIkrimah**: "It (*Jadd*) is the magnificence of our Lord."
- **Qatadah**: "Exalted is His magnificence, His greatness and His command."
- **As-Suddi**: "Exalted is the command of our Lord."
- **Abu Ad-Darda', Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj**: "Exalted is His remembrance (*Dhikr*)."

These read less like competing errors than complementary angles on one reality — His majesty as it stands in itself, as it shows in His acts and commands, as it reaches creation in blessing and favour, and as it is spoken of on tongues. Whichever gloss you take, the word does a single job: putting Allah so far above the creature that what comes next in the ayah becomes unthinkable.

**A small word choice with weight.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to something easy to read past. The jinn do not say *jadduhu*, "*His* majesty," with a third-person pronoun. They keep the name **رَبِّنَا** — *rabbinā*, "our Lord" — expressly retained right there in the sentence. And *rabb* is the attributive name of the One who cherishes and sustains His creation. The point, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, is that the Being who is the Cherisher and Sustainer of His creation must of necessity occupy the lofty position. They could have used shorthand; instead they name Him by the very quality that proves the claim.

**Then the denial.** *Mā ittakhadha ṣāḥibatan wa lā waladā* — "He has taken neither a wife nor a son." Ibn Kathir: "far exalted is He above taking a mate and having children." He then makes the connection explicit — when the jinn accepted Islam and believed in the Qur'an, *this* is what they professed: Allah's magnificence above having taken a spouse and a child.

Notice the order. Majesty first, denial second — and Ibn Kathir's wording ties the two together, that He is *far exalted above* such a thing. To say *taʿālā jadd rabbinā* is already to have said no.

## Ayah 4: naming who started it

**وَأَنَّهُۥ كَانَ يَقُولُ سَفِيهُنَا عَلَى ٱللَّهِ شَطَطًا** — "and that the foolish among us used to utter against Allah that which was an enormity in falsehood."

**Who is "the foolish among us"?** Ibn Kathir reports that **Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, Qatadah and As-Suddi** all said the same thing: "They were referring to **Iblis**." So the jinn trace the lie to its source in their own species — and they do it with a word of contempt, *safīh*, "the foolish one," not a word of awe. Whatever standing he once had over them, in the light of the Qur'an he is simply the fool who spoke falsehood about Allah.

But Ibn Kathir does not let the word stay narrow. He adds that *safīh* "also carries the meaning of everyone in the category who claims that Allah has a spouse or a son." Anyone who says it joins Iblis in the same description. That is a hard sentence to read slowly.

**What is *shaṭaṭ*?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up: *shatat* means "vile words, extravagant or exorbitant or enormous lies," and the word also means "to transgress or act wrongfully, unjustly or exceed the legitimate bounds." So it is not simply an untruth — it is speech that has broken out of its proper limits, gone wildly past where a creature is allowed to go. The early authorities in Ibn Kathir catch both halves: **Abu Malik** (reported by As-Suddi) said "This means a transgression"; **Ibn Zayd** said "A great injustice"; and Ibn Kathir glosses it simply as "falsehood and a lie."

Ibn Kathir also fixes the time frame of *kāna yaqūlu*, "he used to say": this means "before his acceptance of Islam." The past tense is doing repentance work — that was then.

## Ayah 5: the excuse that no longer holds

**وَأَنَّا ظَنَنَّآ أَن لَّن تَقُولَ ٱلۡإِنسُ وَٱلۡجِنُّ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ كَذِبًا** — "And verily, we thought that men and Jinn would not utter a lie against Allah."

Ibn Kathir puts their words into plain speech: "we did not think that humans and Jinns would join each other in lying about Allah by attributing a spouse and a son to Him. So when we heard this Qur'an we believed in it and we knew that they (Jinns and men) had been lying about Allah in this matter."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it as an **excuse being offered**. The believing jinn are explaining how they had ever been involved in disbelief and idolatry in the first place: the foolish people of their nation uttered vile slander against Allah, while they did not think it possible for a human being or a jinn to impute a lie to Allah. They were thus caught up in those foolish people's vile words and committed *kufr* and *shirk* — disbelief, and the setting up of partners alongside Allah. Now they have heard the Qur'an, and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, the reality had later opened up.

**Sit with the mechanism, because it is still running.** Twice in this passage the jinn describe not what they knew but what they *assumed* — "we thought" in ayah 5, "they thought" in ayah 7. Their assumption was not even a cynical one; it was in a way generous. Surely nobody would make things up about Allah. That decent-seeming assumption is exactly what carried them into associating partners with Him. They inherited a claim about Allah from a talker they never examined, and the sheer unthinkability of the lie is what let the lie through.

Note too what broke the spell: not an argument, but **hearing the Qur'an**. They heard it and, in Ibn Kathir's words, they *knew*. Assumption gave way to knowledge the moment the revealed word entered.

## Ayah 6: the valley, and the traffic between the two worlds

**وَأَنَّهُۥ كَانَ رِجَالٞ مِّنَ ٱلۡإِنسِ يَعُوذُونَ بِرِجَالٖ مِّنَ ٱلۡجِنِّ فَزَادُوهُمۡ رَهَقٗا** — "And verily, there were men among mankind who took shelter with the males among the Jinn, but they increased them in *Rahaq*."

**The custom being described.** Ibn Kathir explains that this was the custom of the Arabs in the pre-Islamic days of ignorance: when men would settle in a valley or any place in the wilderness, the open country steppes and other places, they used to seek refuge with the greatest jinn of that particular place so that no harm or evil would afflict them. He gives the human logic with a vivid comparison — like one would do if he entered into the land of his enemies, in the vicinity of a great and powerful man, and sought the protection and guardianship of that man.

**As-Suddi** fills in the scene: "A man used to set out with his family (on a journey) until he came to a piece of land where he would settle. Then he would say, 'I seek refuge with the master (Jinn) of this valley from the Jinns, or that myself, my wealth, my child or my animals are harmed in it.'" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the same custom: people in the Days of Ignorance, when they halted in a valley in the course of a journey, sought refuge in the jinn leader of that valley from the foolish mischief-makers of his nation, believing that the leader of the valley would protect them.

**What did that traffic actually produce?** This is where the ayah turns, and where the commentary is richest — including a genuine difference over *who* increased *whom*.

*Reading one — the jinn increased the humans.* Ibn Kathir takes the speakers to be saying: "we used to think that we had some virtuous status over mankind because they used to seek refuge with us." When the jinn saw that the humans were seeking refuge with them due to their fear of them, they increased them in *rahaq* — which he explains here as fear, terror and fright — and they did this so that the people would be more afraid of them and seek refuge with them even more.

*Reading two — the humans increased the jinn.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders the ayah "they increased them (the Jinns) in arrogance," and explains that this made the jinn think that they are better than human beings, and that it increased the wickedness of the jinn.

**What *rahaq* means.** The early authorities in Ibn Kathir spread across the same range:
- **Qatadah**: "meaning, in sin, and that the Jinns become more bold and daring against them." Elsewhere he adds the sting: "When they sought refuge with them instead of Allah, the Jinns would overcome them with harm because of that."
- **Ibrahim** (reported by Ath-Thawri from Mansur): "the Jinns were courageous and increased in insolence against them."
- **Abu ʿAliyah, Ar-Rabiʿ and Zayd bin Aslam**: "This means in fear."
- **Mujahid**: "The disbelievers would increase in transgression."

So *rahaq* gathers up fear, sin, insolence and transgression — and the readings interlock rather than cancel. Fear made the humans call on the jinn; the calling puffed up the jinn; the puffed-up jinn pressed harder; the harder pressure produced more fear and more sin on both sides. A closed circuit, spinning faster with every turn.

**A narration that captures the whole dynamic.** Ibn Kathir reports that **Ibn Abi Hatim** recorded from **ʿIkrimah** that he said: "The Jinns used to fear humans just like humans fear them, or even worse. So whenever humans would come to a valley the Jinns would flee. So the leader of the people would say, 'We seek refuge with the leader of the inhabitants of this valley.' So the Jinns said, 'We see these people fleeing from us just like we flee from them.' Thus, the Jinns started coming near the humans and afflicting them with insanity and madness."

Read that twice. Both sides were frightened of each other and *both were running away*. It was the humans' act of appealing to the jinn that told the jinn they were feared — and what followed was not protection but affliction. The appeal did not buy safety; it opened the door to harm.

## The story of Rafiʿ ibn ʿUmair

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites from Mazhari's Tafsir, which reports that it is related in *Hawatif-ul-Jinn*, through its chain of narrators, on the authority of **Saʿid ibn Jubayr**, that the Companion **Rafiʿ ibn ʿUmair** described his entry into Islam like this.

He was travelling in a desert one night when sleep overcame him. He alighted from his camel, and before going to sleep he uttered the formula of his people: *"I seek refuge in the leader of the Jinn of this valley from the foolish mischief-makers of his nation."* He then saw in a dream a sword in a person's hand, about to be placed on his camel's chest. He woke in shock, looked around in all directions, found nothing, told himself it was some satanic nightmare, and fell back to sleep — and the same dream came. He got up and looked all around the camel again, found nothing, but this time found the camel shivering. He went back to his place and slept, and the same dream came a third time. He awoke to find the camel tossing about restlessly — and then he saw the youngster with the weapon, the same person he had seen before, his hand held by an old man who was stopping him. Just then three wild zebras appeared, and the old man said to the youngster, "Choose any one of these zebras, and let go this man's camel." The youngster took one of the zebras and took leave.

Then the old man looked at Rafiʿ and said, "You fool, when you seek refuge in a valley, and you fear any danger from the jinn or devils, recite thus:"

> **اعوذ باللہ ربِّ محمّد من ھول ھٰذا الوادی**
> *"I seek refuge in Allah, the Lord of Muhammad, from the horrors of this valley."*

"Do not seek refuge in any Jinn because that time is gone when human beings used to seek refuge in Jinn."

Rafiʿ asked who that person was. The old man replied that he was the Arabian Prophet ﷺ, neither eastern nor western; that he was raised with his Prophetic mission on a Monday; and that he lived in Yathrib, an area where dates grow abundantly. As soon as morning dawned, Rafiʿ set out for Madinah, urging his mount faster and faster until he reached it — and when the Prophet ﷺ saw him, he recounted the entire episode to him before Rafiʿ could tell him anything. He then invited him to the call of Islam, and Rafiʿ embraced the faith.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr said that ayah 6 was revealed in this connection.

Whatever weight one gives the chain of such a report, notice what the story is *for* in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's hands: it dramatises the exact correction the ayah is making. The old formula named a jinn; the new formula names **Allah**, identified as *the Lord of Muhammad* — the very Prophet ﷺ whose Qur'an, ayah 1 told us, a group of jinn listened to and believed in. And the closing line is the whole point of the passage in a sentence: *that time is gone.*

## Ayah 7: the assumption both species shared

**وَأَنَّهُمۡ ظَنُّواْ كَمَا ظَنَنتُمۡ أَن لَّن يَبۡعَثَ ٱللَّهُ أَحَدًا** — "And they thought as you thought, that Allah will not send any Messenger."

Ibn Kathir gives the sense: Allah would never send a Messenger after this long period of time. This, he notes, is what **Al-Kalbi** and **Ibn Jarir** said.

The ayah puts humans and jinn shoulder to shoulder in one indictment — "they thought, **as you thought**" — and it is the same verb of assumption from ayah 5. The two species had lied about Allah together, and now we learn they had given up on Him together too. Long silence had been read as permanent silence. Nothing had come for generations, so nothing would come.

And that is why it is the perfect note to end this stretch of their testimony on. The passage began with the jinn hearing a recitation (ayah 1) and ends with them confessing they had assumed no such recitation would ever arrive. The assumption is refuted by the very thing they are standing there talking about.

## What this asks of us

**Take refuge only with Allah.** The custom in ayah 6 belongs to the pre-Islamic desert, but its logic does not: fear something, look for a nearer, more visible protector, and end up owned by whatever you appealed to. Qatadah's sentence is worth memorising — when they sought refuge with them *instead of Allah*, the jinn would overcome them with harm because of that. The very thing they turned to for safety became the source of their injury.

**Examine what you have been told about Allah.** The jinn's excuse in ayah 5 — *we never imagined anyone would lie about Allah* — did not save them from having lived in disbelief and idolatry. Ibn Kathir's expansion of *safīh* to include everyone who claims that Allah has a spouse or a son means the responsibility is not confined to Iblis; it reaches the repeaters. Claims about Allah are the one area where inherited confidence is least safe and where the criterion — the Qur'an itself — is nearest to hand.

**Be careful what you feed.** ʿIkrimah's narration and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's reading both show something being *fed* by the attention paid to it: the jinn came to think themselves better than human beings, and their wickedness increased.

**And do not mistake delay for absence.** The mistake in ayah 7 was to convert "nothing has come for a long time" into "nothing will come." Allah's silence is never His indifference — and the jinn of this surah found that out in the most direct way possible: a group of them listened, and what they heard was a wonderful Recitation that guides to the right path.

passages.title: The guarded heaven and the end of eavesdropping
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah al-Jinn 72:8–10

These three ayat are the jinn's own testimony about the night their world changed. Before this, they had free access to the news of the heavens; one night they found the way barred — guards everywhere, and flames. Ayah 8 reports the discovery, ayah 9 states the new rule that replaced their old arrangement, and ayah 10 admits, with striking honesty, that they could not yet tell what it all meant. Discovery, rule, question — and the question is the hinge, because the answer turned out to be a man standing in prayer in Makkah, reciting.

## What they used to do

Before we can feel what ayah 8 is reporting, we need to know what they lost.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān brings two narrations. The first, which Maʿārif cites through Mazhari, is reported in the Sahih of Bukhari on the authority of Sayyidah ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her): the angels descend in the *ʿanān* of the sky — meaning the cloud — and there they mention the matter that has been decreed in the sky; the devils listen in on their private conversation without the angels knowing about it, then carry what they caught to the soothsayers, mixing it "with a hundred lies from their side."

The second is recorded in the Sahih of Bukhari on the authority of Sayyidunā Abū Hurayrah, and in Muslim on the authority of Sayyidunā Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with them): when Allah issues an order in the sky, the angels flap their wings in readiness to obey it; once the issuing is complete they discuss it among themselves — and the devils eavesdrop on that discussion and pass it to the soothsayers, admixed with many lies.

That last detail is the mechanism both narrations describe. What reached the soothsayer was not pure invention: there was a real fragment in it, stolen from a conversation of angels. But it arrived wrapped in a hundred lies of the devils' own making.

## Sky, or cloud?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a precise question about the word *samā'* in ayah 8. In Arabic it is used in two senses: "sky" and also "cloud". Here, Maʿārif says, it would appear to be the second — the jinn were not going inside the heavens but going up to the clouds and taking up positions there to sit and eavesdrop.

The two narrations look, at first glance, as though they disagree: ʿĀ'ishah's report places the eavesdropping at the cloud, while the other speaks of an order issued in the sky. Maʿārif answers that in fact there is no conflict, and that the second narration does not prove the devils went inside the sky at all: probably the order, once issued by Allah, filters down through the angels from the upper level to the lower, until the angels come down to the cloud and discuss it there — and that is where the devils steal it, exactly as ʿĀ'ishah reported.

## The words of ayat 8 and 9

**"Stern guards"** — *ḥarasan shadīdan*. Not a patrol, but a filling. Ibn Kathir says Allah filled the sky with stern guards "guarding it from all of its sides." Every side is covered.

**"Sitting stations"** — *maqāʿid*, in ayah 9. Both commentaries stress how settled this was. Ibn Kathir says the devils "had taken sitting stations for themselves in the heaven of this world and they would listen to the matters that occurred in the heaven." Maʿārif says they used to position themselves in the cloud and eavesdrop on the conversations of the angels, having "free access to the heavenly information." This was not the odd break-in. It was an established arrangement with places of their own.

**"Now"** — *al-āna*, in the middle of ayah 9. One small word marks the change. What comes before it is the old arrangement; what comes after it is the new one. *Whoever listens now* — the jinn are not describing a bad night. Ibn Kathir says the devils were expelled from the places where they used to sit prior to that.

**"A flame lying in wait"** — *shihāban raṣadan*. Ibn Kathir's gloss is uncompromising: whoever would like to steal some information by listening "will find a flaming fire waiting in ambush for him. It will not pass him or miss him, but it will wipe him out and destroy him completely." The flame is not a warning shot. It is posted, aimed, and certain.

## The night it happened

Ibn Kathir tells the story, and it is worth having in full.

Shooting stars, he notes, had occurred before this — however it did not happen much, rather only occasionally. He reports the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: while we were sitting with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ a shooting star flashed in the sky, and the Prophet ﷺ asked, *"What did you all used to say about this?"* They replied, "We used to say that a great person has been born and a great person has died." He ﷺ said, *"This is not so, rather whenever Allah decrees a matter in the heaven…"* — and Ibn Kathir notes that the rest of the hadith continues from there, having already been given in full under Sūrah Saba'.

Then Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ as a Prophet and Messenger, and the devils, who had taken sitting stations for themselves in the heaven of this world, were suddenly pelted one night.

The effect on earth was terror. Ibn Kathir writes that when so many shooting stars began appearing in the sky, it horrified humans and jinn alike; they were disturbed and alarmed, and thought that it was the destruction of the world. In Ṭā'if, people seeing the severe fires in the sky and the shooting flames began saying, "The dwellers of the sky have been destroyed." They began freeing their servants and abandoning their luxuries. Then ʿAbd Yālayl bin ʿAmr bin ʿUmayr — who was referred to for judgement among them — said: "Woe to you O people of Ṭā'if! Hold on to your wealth and look at these guiding stars in the sky. If you see them remaining in their place, then the dwellers of the sky have not been destroyed, rather this has happened because of Ibn Abī Kabshah" — meaning Muhammad ﷺ. "And if you look and see that you can no longer see these stars, then verily the dwellers of the sky have been destroyed." They looked, the stars still remained, and they kept their wealth.

The devils were frightened that night too. They went to Iblīs and informed him of what had happened. He said, "Bring me a handful of dirt from every land so that I may smell it." They brought it, he smelled it, and said: "It is your friend in Makkah." He then sent a group of seven jinn to Makkah, and they found the Prophet of Allah ﷺ standing in prayer in Al-Masjid Al-Ḥarām while reciting the Qur'an. They drew near to him, eager to hear the Qur'an, until their chests almost pressed against him. Then they accepted Islam, and Allah revealed their matter to His Messenger ﷺ.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the same search from the jinn's side: the barring of the upper region was a new phenomenon that excited their curiosity, so they divided themselves into groups and went to the east and to the west to investigate, and one group arrived at a place called Nakhlah where its members heard the Qur'an and embraced Islam. Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: they set out searching in the east and the west, then found the Messenger of Allah ﷺ reciting while leading his Companions in prayer — and *thus they knew that this Qur'an was the reason for the sky being guarded.* Some among them believed in it; the others became more rebellious in their transgression. He connects this to Allah's statement in Sūrat al-Aḥqāf: **"And when We sent towards you a group of the Jinn, (quietly) listening to the Qur'an"** (46:29).

## Why the sky was sealed

Ibn Kathir states the purpose directly. Allah sent His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ and revealed the Qur'an to him, and among the ways He protected it was by filling the sky with stern guards on every side. The devils were expelled from the places where they used to sit **so that they could not steal anything from the Qur'an and tell it to the soothsayers**, thereby causing matters to be confused and mixed up — and, in Ibn Kathir's words, if this happened "it would not be known who was being truthful."

Sit with that for a moment. Revelation was descending, and the one channel by which stolen news had always reached the fortune-tellers was still open. Ibn Kathir names the sealing of it for what it is: Allah did this "out of His kindness to His creation, His mercy upon His servants and His protection of His Mighty Book."

Maʿārif adds the same logic from the other end: at the advent of the Prophet ﷺ there arose the need to protect the heavenly revelation, so the devils' access to the upper region was stopped in such a way that any devil who attempted to go up would be repelled by piercing flames.

As-Suddī, cited by Ibn Kathir, states the general principle: "The sky was never guarded except if there was a Prophet in the earth or the religion of Allah was victorious and dominant in the earth."

## But meteors are older than Islam

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the objection honestly. The existence of meteors — *inqiḍāḍ al-kawkab*, "falling stars" in common parlance — is not a new phenomenon; yet this ayah indicates they showed up to repel the devils as though they were something new that came with the Prophet ﷺ.

The answer given is careful, and worth learning as a model for handling this kind of question. There is no denying that meteors did exist since the inception of time and space, before his ﷺ advent, and there is no contradiction between what humanity has experienced since the beginning of the world, scientific explanations, and the Qur'anic statement. Maʿārif even summarises what philosophers and scientists say: meteors may originate from the earth or stars or disintegrating planets, wandering in space at enormous speeds and falling to the earth; some fiery matter may arise from the surface of the earth and heat up, or the speed of the meteors makes them glow and burn, or a flame is emitted from a star — and this may have habitually continued ever since.

The point of the ayah is not the existence of the flames but their **employment**. Before the Prophet ﷺ, these flames were not used to serve a particular purpose; they were merely a natural phenomenon. After his advent, meteoric flames were used to serve the purpose of shooting the devils if they attempted to go up and listen furtively to the conversation of the angels. The same created thing was given a new commission. (Maʿārif refers the reader to its own longer treatment under 15:17–18.)

## Ayah 10: the honesty of not knowing

Then comes the line that gives this passage its moral beauty. **"And we know not whether evil is intended for those on the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance."**

Ibn Kathir explains the sense: we do not know if this — the matter which has occurred in the sky — is intended for those who are in the earth, or if their Lord intends some guidance for them.

Maʿārif spells out the two readings the jinn were weighing. The jinn and devils have been barred from heavenly news; in that case this could be a punishment for the inhabitants of the earth. However, if Allah intends them to be rightly guided, then He has barred the jinn and shayāṭīn from access to the heaven precisely so that they do not interfere with divine revelation. Same event, two opposite meanings — and the jinn, at that stage, expressed their reservations honestly: they had no idea which it was.

Now look at *how* they said it, because Ibn Kathir draws attention to it. The evil is mentioned without it being attributed to anyone at all; the guidance is attributed by name to **their Lord**. Ibn Kathir says they stated it in such a manner out of their etiquette in phrasing their speech, "because they did not attribute the doing of evil to anyone and they attributed the good to Allah." And he grounds this manner of speech in the Sunnah, citing what has been recorded in the Sahih: **"And evil is not attributed to You."**

So this is not merely good manners; it is a way of speaking that the Sunnah itself teaches. Good is named to Allah; evil is spoken of without pinning it on Him. Jinn who had spent their careers stealing conversations spoke about Allah with that much care — and the Qur'an records their words.

## Living it

**Your Qur'an came guarded.** Ibn Kathir says the sky was filled with stern guards on every side so that nothing of this revelation could be stolen and passed to the soothsayers. He calls that kindness, mercy, and protection. Every time you open the muṣḥaf, you are holding something that was protected at that cost.

**Soothsaying was never a rival source of truth.** The two narrations in Maʿārif show exactly how the trade worked: a stolen scrap, then a hundred lies. That should permanently settle how a believer regards fortune-tellers and anyone claiming private access to the unseen — even the sliver of truth in it was stolen goods, and whoever tries to listen now, Ibn Kathir says, finds a flame lying in ambush.

**The Prophet ﷺ corrected the folk explanation of the sky.** People said a shooting star meant a great person had been born or died; he ﷺ said this is not so, and tied it instead to Allah's decreeing a matter in the heaven. Believers do not read omens into events. We read them back to the One who decreed them.

**Say it the way they said it.** Ascribe the good to Allah by name; do not pin evil on Him. That is the adab of ayah 10, and it costs nothing but attention.

**Curiosity, followed honestly, ends at the Qur'an.** The jinn did not shrug the sign off. They said "we know not", and then they went searching — east and west — until they found a man reciting in prayer, and knew that this Qur'an was the reason the sky was being guarded. Ibn Kathir notes that even then the response split two ways: some believed in it, and others became more rebellious in their transgression. The sign was the same for everyone. What differed was what each one did with it.

passages.title: Jinn divided into submitters and deviants
passages.tafsir:
**The jinn take their own measure.** The jinn who overheard the Qur'an are still speaking, still reporting back to their people — and here they turn the lens from what they heard onto who they are. Their report becomes an honest self-audit: our kind is not one thing, we cannot escape our Lord, we believed the moment guidance reached us — and so we fall into two groups with two very different ends.

That movement is what binds ayat 11–15 into one unit: an admission of internal difference (11), a confession of Allah's inescapable power (12), the response they actually made when guidance came (13), and then the sorting of all that difference into a final, named division with a verdict attached (14–15). Ibn Kathir heads this whole section with a single sentence: "The Jinns testify that among Them there are Believers, Disbelievers, Misguided and Guided."

## Ayah 11 — "Some are righteous, and some the contrary"

Notice how carefully they phrase it. They name the good side plainly — *al-ṣāliḥūn*, the righteous — but the other side they do not name at all. They say **dūna dhālik**, which Ibn Kathir glosses simply as "other than that"; the translation on this page renders it "those who are less." It is the language of a community admitting a fault it is not yet ready to spell out.

Then comes the summary: **kunnā ṭarā'iqa qidadā** — "we are groups having different ways." Ibn Kathir explains this as being "on numerous differing paths and having different thoughts and opinions," so the difference among them is not only in conduct but in conviction — how they think, what they hold to be true. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others cut straight to it: "This means among us are believers and among us are disbelievers."

**A note on how Ibn Kathir illustrates this.** Commenting on this ayah, Ibn Kathir cites a curious report — not a prophetic hadith, but a story told about the early scholar Al-A'mash, reported by Ahmad bin Sulayman An-Najjad in his book of *Amālī*. Al-A'mash said a jinn came to them; he asked what food is most beloved to their kind and was told rice, and when rice was brought he saw the morsels being lifted but saw no hand lifting them. He then asked the jinn whether they have among their kind the same desires — that is, religious innovations — as humans have among theirs, and the jinn said yes. Ibn Kathir adds that he presented this chain of narration to "our Shaykh, Al-Ḥāfiẓ Abī Al-Ḥajjāj Al-Mizzī," who said its chain is authentic to Al-A'mash.

## Ayah 12 — Nowhere on earth, and no use running

**"And we think that we cannot escape Allah in the earth, nor can we escape Him by flight."**

The verb they use, *ẓanannā*, is the ordinary Arabic word for supposing or thinking — yet Ibn Kathir renders their meaning as knowledge, not guesswork: "we know that the power of Allah is decisive over us and that we cannot escape Him in the earth. Even if we try to flee, we know that He has complete control over us and that none of us can escape Him." The translation on this page reflects that same certainty: "we truly know."

They close off two escapes, not one. *Fī al-arḍ* — not in the earth; *haraban* — and not by flight. Ibn Kathir presses both halves: no escape where they are, and no escape by fleeing.

As background, the commentary *Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān* — a tafsir, that is, a work of Qur'anic explanation — notes in connection with the preceding ayah that the jinn and the devils had been barred from access to heavenly news, so that they would not interfere with the divine revelation being sent down. The sky had already been closed to them; here they acknowledge that the earth is no refuge either.

Note also what kind of statement this is. It is not a theory argued from evidence; it is a confession from beings who tested the limits and found them absolute — that Allah's power over them is decisive and His control complete.

## Ayah 13 — Heard it, believed it

**"And indeed when we heard the Guidance, we believed therein."**

There is no gap in that sentence. Hearing and believing sit side by side with nothing in between — the translation on this page catches it with a single added word: they "˹readily˺ believed." Ibn Kathir says of this line that they were proud of it, "and it is something for them to be proud of, as well as a great honor for them and a good characteristic." That is a striking thing for a commentator to say about jinn: their response to guidance is counted to their credit and named an honour.

**And then the promise.** *Fa-man yu'min bi-rabbihi falā yakhāfu bakhsan wa lā rahaqā* — "whosoever believes in his Lord shall have no fear, either of a decrease in the reward of his good deeds or an increase in the punishment for his sins."

Observe that they do not confine this to themselves. They shift to *man* — "whoever" — and state it as a standing rule: whoever believes in his Lord. Jinn or human, the wording is one.

Two words carry the meaning, and the sources open both:

- **Bakhs.** *Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān* notes it is vowelled *bakhs* (with fatḥa on the *bā'* and sukūn on the *khā'*) and means "to reduce the right" — to shortchange someone of what is genuinely theirs.
- **Rahaq.** *Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān* gives its sense as "disgrace," and sums up the ayah this way: anyone who believes in Allah need fear neither curtailment in the reward of his good deeds, nor disgrace by excess in his punishment in the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others explain the phrase in the same direction: the believer "should not fear that the reward for his good deeds will be decreased or that he will be burdened with anything other than his sins."

Put the two together and you have the exact pair of fears any honest person carries into a reckoning: *that what I earned will be quietly trimmed*, and *that what I never did will be piled onto me*. The ayah rules out both. Ibn Kathir places beside it Allah's words in Sūrah Ṭā Hā: "Then he will have no fear of injustice, nor of any curtailment" (20:112).

What is being promised is not exemption from the reckoning — the believer still carries his own sins into it. What is promised is that nothing earned will be reduced and nothing unearned will be added.

## Ayah 14 — Muslims, and Qāsiṭūn

**"And of us some are Muslims, and of us some are Al-Qāsiṭūn."**

Here the euphemism of ayah 11 is dropped. What was "other than that" is now named. And the naming turns on a piece of Arabic worth pausing over. Ibn Kathir defines it precisely: "The Qāsiṭ is he who behaves unjustly with the truth and deviates from it. This is the opposite of the Muqsiṭ, the one who is just."

So the line drawn here is a line of justice. On one side stands the *muqsiṭ*, the one who is just; on the other the *qāsiṭ*, who deals unjustly with the truth and swerves away from it. One community, two directions.

The pairing itself is worth noticing. The alternative to *muslim* is not stated as a bare label of unbelief but as *qāsiṭ* — and on Ibn Kathir's definition, that is a description of conduct toward the truth: refusing to give it its due.

**"And whosoever has embraced Islam, then such have sought the right path."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is beautifully practical: "they sought salvation for themselves." Islam here is described as an act of seeking — *taḥarraw rashadā*, they aimed for and pursued *rashad*, right guidance. It is what a person does on his own behalf, for his own rescue.

## Ayah 15 — Firewood

**"And as for the Qāsiṭūn, they shall be firewood for Hell."**

Ibn Kathir: "meaning, fuel, for they will be used to kindle it (the Fire)."

Firewood is not simply a thing that gets burned. Firewood is what makes the fire burn — what feeds it and keeps it going. On Ibn Kathir's reading the image is not of a punishment merely applied to them from outside: they are what the Fire is kindled with.

## What these ayat settle about the jinn

Taken together, and without adding anything from outside them, ayat 11–15 tell us a great deal. The jinn are a mixed creation, not uniformly evil: among them are the righteous and among them are those "other than that." They can hear revelation and respond to it with faith. They are under Allah's decisive power with no possibility of escape. They are sorted by the same criterion we are — submission — and those of them who deal unjustly with the truth end as fuel for the Fire. The believers among them fall under the same promise of a fair reckoning stated in ayah 13, since that promise is worded for "whoever believes in his Lord."

## Living it

The jinn have handed us a way of speaking about our own community that is rare and worth borrowing.

**They did not idealise their own people.** Their report opens by admitting that their nation contains the righteous and those other than that — differing paths, differing thoughts and opinions. Honest self-description came first; only then could anything true be said about destinies.

**They did not hide behind the group either.** Having said "we are groups having different ways," they immediately shift in ayah 13 to *man yu'min* — "whoever believes." A mixed community does not dilute individual responsibility. Nobody is judged by the average of his people.

**They closed the gap between hearing and answering.** Ibn Kathir counts their response to guidance an honour to them and a good characteristic. The distance between "I heard the guidance" and "I believed in it" is the space in which most people lose themselves — a delay, a wait for a better moment, a look around to see who else is moving.

**They knew where the fear belongs.** A believer's proper fear, according to ayah 13, is not that he will be shortchanged or disgraced — that is ruled out. What remains, in the words of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, is his own sins and nothing besides.

**And the sorting line is submission.** Ayah 14 divides an entire creation we cannot even see by exactly the criterion that divides us: *fa-man aslama* — whoever submits.

The passage continues in ayat 16–17.

passages.title: Rain as a trial, turning away as ruin
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** The jinn have finished speaking about themselves; now the speech is Allah's own. Ibn Kathir gives the two ayat as: *"If they had believed in Allah, and went on the way, We would surely have bestowed on them water in abundance. That We might try them thereby. And whosoever turns away from the Reminder of his Lord, He will cause him to enter in a Sa'ad torment."* Our translation renders the opening, "Had the deniers followed the Right Way…", and the second ayah, "as a test for them. And whoever turns away from the remembrance…"

**What binds the two ayat into one unit** is the phrase at the head of ayah 17: *li-naftinahum fīhi*, "That We might try them thereby." It reaches back and takes hold of the abundance promised in ayah 16 and names what it is — a test. Then the rest of ayah 17 announces the outcome for the one who turns away: not merely the loss of the water, but a torment Ibn Kathir describes as having no relaxation in it.

**Who is "they"?** The ayah opens with a pronoun, and the sentence just before it, ayah 15, has named the *qāsiṭūn* — those who, in Ibn Kathir's definition, behave unjustly with the truth and deviate from it — saying they shall be firewood for Hell, which he glosses as "fuel, for they will be used to kindle it (the Fire)." When Ibn Kathir comes to ayah 16 he begins his first explanation with exactly that group: "if **the deviant ones** would stand firmly upon the path of Islam…" So the "they" of ayah 16 carries the deviant ones of the preceding sentence into this new statement.

## Ayah 16: the words

**"If they had believed in Allah, and went on the way."** Ibn Kathir's paraphrase on his first reading is worth having in full, because he piles up the verbs: that they "would stand firmly upon the path of Islam, being just upon it and remaining upon it." Not a moment of straightness, then — standing, being just, remaining. All three.

**"We would surely have bestowed on them water in abundance"** — *māʾan ghadaqā*. Ibn Kathir glosses *ghadaq* with two words: "a lot." And he does not leave the image at rainfall. He says at once: "The intent behind this is to say that they would be given an abundance of sustenance." Rain here stands for provision as a whole — what comes in, what feeds you, what makes life easy.

## The great fork: two readings of ayah 16

Here Ibn Kathir does something a careful reader should notice. He writes: "The commentators have differed over the explanation of this. There are two views concerning it." He then lays both out at length, and in this passage he does not pronounce a winner. Where the scholars genuinely differed, the honest thing is to report the difference rather than flatten it.

**The first view: "the way" is the path of Islam.** If the deviant ones had stood firm on the path of Islam, they would have been given an abundance of sustenance — and then tested by it. The testing is spelled out by Zayd ibn Aslam, as Mālik reported from him: *"That We might try them* — means, so that We may test them to see who will remain upon the guidance from those who will turn back to sin." Ibn Kathir's own gloss on the phrase is just as bare: "We will test them."

Ibn Kathir then names the weight of authority behind this reading: al-ʿAwfī reported similar to it from Ibn ʿAbbas, and likewise said Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, ʿAṭāʾ, as-Suddī, Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī, Qatādah and aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk.

**The second view: "the way" is the way of misguidance.** On this reading, "if they had… went on the way" means the way of error — and the abundant water is not a reward at all. Ibn Kathir's words: "then We would have increased their sustenance to allow a gradual respite." That is, wealth handed to the heedless as rope, not as rescue. He anchors this with two other ayat of the Qur'an. First, 6:44 — "So, when they forgot that with which they had been reminded, We opened for them the gates of everything, until in the midst of their enjoyment in that which they were given, all of a sudden, We took them, and lo! They were plunged into destruction with deep regrets and sorrows." Then 23:55–56 — "Do they think that in wealth and children with which We expand them. We hasten unto them with good things. Nay, but they perceive not."

This is the view of Abū Mijlaz, and Ibn Kathir says it agrees with the opinion of Ibn Ḥumayd, who said of the phrase: "This means the path of misguidance." Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim both recorded it. Al-Baghawī also mentioned it from ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Kalbī and Ibn Kaysān — and Ibn Kathir adds, "It seems that he (Al-Baghawī) took this position." Its supporting argument, Ibn Kathir notes, is the very next phrase of the Qur'an itself: "And it is supported by Allah's saying, 'That We might try them thereby.'" If the water were pure reward, why would the ayah immediately call it a trial?

(A small detail that shows how alive this discussion was: Zayd ibn Aslam appears on **both** sides of Ibn Kathir's account — his gloss on "That We might try them" is quoted under the first view, while al-Baghawī names him among those who held the second.)

**What both readings share.** Ibn Kathir sets the two out as competing explanations of what "the way" refers to, and leaves them standing. But notice that both of them run through the same phrase, *That We might try them thereby*: the first view reads it as the test that follows the reward, and the second view uses it as the proof that the giving was never a reward in the first place. Whichever way a reader leans, the ayah's own next words call the abundance a trial. That much is not in dispute between them.

## The setting: seven years without rain

In the course of listing those who held the first view, Ibn Kathir preserves a report that grounds all this in a hard memory. Muqātil said: "This Ayah was revealed about the disbelievers of the Quraysh when they were deprived of rain for seven years."

If that is the setting, then the ayah is speaking to men standing in a drought, being told that the rain they are desperate for is bound up with the way they walk — and that even in abundance it would be a test, not a settlement. It is worth noticing, too, that on Muqātil's report this ayah addresses the disbelievers of Quraysh, human beings, even though the ayat just before it were quoting the jinn.

## Ayah 17: turning away, and a punishment that will not relent

**"That We might try them thereby."** The phrase governs everything before it. Ibn Kathir's explanation is three words long — "We will test them" — and Zayd ibn Aslam's fills in the shape of the test: who will remain upon the guidance, and who will turn back to sin. Notice what the ayah does *not* say. It does not say the abundance is given as an approval, or as a punishment. It is given so that they may be tried by it: a gift with a question inside it.

**"And whosoever turns away from the Reminder of his Lord."** Ibn Kathir's rendering says "the Reminder"; our translation of the ayah says "the remembrance" — the revelation that reminds, and the remembering it is meant to produce. And the ayah does not describe a man who attacks the Reminder or argues it down. It describes one who simply *turns away* — presents his back, lets it go past him. That is all the failure this ayah needs to name.

**"He will cause him to enter in a *Sa'ad* torment."** Ibn Kathir explains it: "a harsh, severe, agonizing and painful punishment." Then he gathers the reports of the early authorities on this strange word *ṣaʿadā*:

- Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Qatādah and Ibn Zayd all said: "This means harsh having no relaxation in it." That last clause is the sting of it — not simply severe, but severe with no let-up, no pause, no breathing space anywhere inside it.
- "It has also been reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said, 'It is a mountain in Hell.'"
- "It has been related from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr that he said, 'It is a well in Hell.'"

Ibn Kathir sets these down one after another and does not rule between them. The reader is left with the word's weight rather than a single picture of it.

## Living it

**Never read your provision as a verdict.** Whichever of the two views one takes, these ayat forbid the equation "things are going well, therefore Allah is pleased with me." On the first view abundance is given to the straight and then tests them. On the second it is sustenance increased "to allow a gradual respite" — exactly what 6:44 describes, the gates of everything opened, and then the sudden seizure at the height of enjoyment.

**And do not read hardship as a verdict either.** In Muqātil's report the Quraysh were without rain for seven years, and the ayah's answer to their drought is not despair but direction: it points them to the way — and warns that even abundance would only be a further examination.

**Ask Zayd ibn Aslam's question of yourself.** His gloss is really a diagnostic: when the provision came, did you remain upon the guidance, or turn back to sin? The honest use of these ayat is to look at what your last increase in income, health, or ease actually did to your prayer, your tongue, and your generosity.

**Guard against mere turning away.** Ayah 17 does not require enmity to earn its warning. Drifting from the Reminder — not reading it, not sitting with it, letting the days pass without it — is precisely the turning away the ayah names. And the remedy is as plain as the diagnosis: turn back toward the remembrance of your Lord, since the whole passage is built to make you do exactly that while the choice is still yours.

passages.title: Worship for Allah alone; the Prophet only conveys
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** The sūrah opened with the words *"Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of jinn listened"* (72:1). Here it arrives at the point all that listening was aimed at: worship belongs to Allah alone, and the man at the centre of the scene holds no power of his own — he is a servant with a message to deliver.

These seven ayat move as one arc. Ayah 18 lays down the rule: the *masājid* are Allah's, so call on no one beside Him. Ayah 19 sets a scene — a crowd pressing in around "the servant of Allah" as he stood calling upon Him — which the early scholars read in three quite different ways. Then come three commands of "Say" (ayat 20, 21, 22), in which the Prophet ﷺ strips away, one by one, every power people might imagine belongs to him; ayah 23 continues the last of them, until nothing is left in his hands but the message itself. Ayah 24 closes with a promise about who will turn out, on the day it is counted properly, to be the weaker and smaller party.

## Ayah 18: "The places of worship belong to Allah"

**Two ways to read masājid.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the key word. Read the ordinary way, *masājid* is the plural of *masjid* — mosques, places of worship dedicated for the performance of prayers. The verse then means that all mosques belong to Allah, dedicated to His sole worship, so we are not permitted to call on anyone else besides Allah, the way the Jews and Christians commit shirk in their places of worship. As Maʿārif sums it up, the mosques must be kept clear of all false beliefs and vile deeds.

Maʿārif adds that the word could carry another sense. It could be the plural of *masjad*, with a *fatḥa* on the *jīm* — in which case, says Maʿārif, it is a *masdar mīmī*, a grammatical category the tafsir glosses simply as "infinitivity," and the word means "to prostrate or prostration" rather than the place where prostration happens. Read this way, the verse signifies that worship is reserved exclusively for Allah: it is not permitted to prostrate to anyone. And Maʿārif draws the line that makes the rest of the ayah click into place — if a person calls on anyone else for help, it is as though he is prostrating to him, which must be avoided.

**Qatadah on why this was said.** Qatadah said that whenever the Jews and Christians used to enter their churches and synagogues, they would associate partners with Allah; so Allah commanded His Prophet ﷺ to tell them that they should single Him out alone for worship.

**The jinn's question.** Ibn Jarir recorded from Saʿīd bin Jubayr a moment that makes the ayah personal. The jinn said to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ: "How can we come to the Masjid while we are distant — meaning very far away — from you? And how can we be present for the prayer while we are far away from you?" So Allah revealed this ayah.

Read the answer against the question. They asked about *distance from him*, and the reply does not mention him at all: the masājid are Allah's, and no one is to be invoked along with Him. The One worshipped there is not tied to a building or to a person's presence. It is a gentle redirection — and redirection away from the Prophet ﷺ and toward Allah is exactly what the ayat that follow will say outright.

## Ayah 19: the crowding, and three ways to understand it

Ibn Kathir's text renders the ayah: "And when the servant of Allah (*ʿabd Allāh*) stood up invoking Him in prayer they just made round him a dense crowd as if sticking one over the other." The Arabic clause ends on the word *libadan* — bodies packed and piled. All three of the explanations Ibn Kathir cites take the one standing to be the Prophet ﷺ, and it is worth pausing on the title the ayah gives him: at the very moment a crowd is pressing around him, he is named not "the Messenger" but "the servant of Allah" — standing and calling on his Lord like any worshipper.

Who was crowding, and in what spirit? Ibn Kathir lays out three views.

**One: the jinn, out of eagerness.** Al-ʿAwfī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that when they heard the Prophet ﷺ reciting the Qur'an "they almost mounted on top of him due to their zeal." They drew very near to him, and he was unaware of them until the messenger — that is, Jibrīl — came to him and made him recite, *"Say: It has been revealed to me that a group of Jinn listened"* (72:1). They were listening to the Qur'an. On this reading the crowd is an adoring press of unseen listeners, and the ayah loops back to the opening of the sūrah. Ibn Kathir notes that this opinion has also been reported from Az-Zubayr bin Al-ʿAwwām.

**Two: the jinn describing what they saw.** Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn ʿAbbās that these are the jinn's own words, said to their people. When they saw him praying and his Companions were bowing with his bowing and prostrating with his prostrating, they were amazed at his Companions' obedience to him — and so they reported it to their people in these terms. Here the crowding is the ranks of the congregation, and what struck the jinn was the discipline of a body of people moving as one. This second view has also been reported from Saʿīd bin Jubayr.

**Three: humans and jinn massing against him.** Al-Hasan said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up and said none has the right to be worshipped except Allah, and he called the people to their Lord, the Arabs almost crowded over him together (against him)." Qatadah said: "Humans and Jinns both crowded together over this matter in order to extinguish it. However, Allah insisted upon helping it, supporting it and making it victorious over those who opposed it." This third view has also been reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd bin Jubayr and Ibn Zayd; it was the view preferred by Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Kathir says it "seems to be the most apparent meaning of the Ayah."

**Why Ibn Kathir prefers the third.** His stated reason is what comes immediately after: Allah's statement in ayah 20, *"Say: I invoke only my Lord, and I associate none as partners along with Him"* — which reads as a reply to hostility rather than to admiration. Notice how much a single interpretive choice changes the emotional temperature of the same words: a rapt audience, an orderly congregation, or a mob closing in.

## Ayat 20–23: the "Say"s that empty his hands

**Ayah 20 — the answer to pressure is tawḥīd.** Ibn Kathir sets the scene: when they harmed him, opposed him, denied him and stood against him in order to thwart the truth he came with, and to unite against him, the Messenger ﷺ said to them, *"I invoke only my Lord, and I associate none as partners along with Him."* Ibn Kathir explains the first half as: "I only worship my Lord alone, and He has no partners. I seek His help and I put my trust in Him."

The reply is not a threat and not a defence. It is a restatement of the same creed that caused the trouble. And notice the same word running through both ayat: ayah 18 says *"invoke not anyone along with Allah,"* and here he says *"I invoke only my Lord."* He is not asking of them anything he does not do himself.

**Ayah 21 — no power over harm, no power over guidance.** *"It is not in my power to cause you harm, or to bring you to the right path"* — the word rendered "the right path" is *rashad*, right guidance; the translation on this page renders the pair as "harm or benefit." Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is worth reading slowly: "I am only a man like you all and I have received revelation. I am only a servant among the servants of Allah. I have no control over the affairs of your guidance or your misguidance. Rather all of these things are referred to Allah."

This dismantles the very assumption a crowding throng makes — that the man at the centre is a source of harm or of benefit in himself. He is not. He is a servant who was given a revelation.

**Ayah 22 — and no safety for himself either.** Having removed his power over them, he removes any pretence of security for himself: none can protect him from Allah's punishment, nor can he find refuge except in Him. As Ibn Kathir puts it, the Prophet ﷺ says about himself that no one can save him from Allah either — "if I disobey Allah, then no one would be able to rescue me from His punishment." On the word *multaḥad* (rendered "refuge"), Mujāhid, Qatādah and As-Suddī all said it means "No place to escape to."

Hold the two halves of the ayah together: there is no shelter *from* Allah, and no shelter anywhere *but* in Allah. The only refuge from Him is Him.

**Ayah 23 — the one thing left in his hands.** Ibn Kathir reads *illā balāghan*, "(Mine is) but conveyance from Allah and His Messages," as an exception related to the previous statement, "None can protect me from Allah's punishment" — meaning: nothing can save me from Him and rescue me except my conveyance of the Message that He has obligated me to carry out. So the sole refuge is obedience, and the specific obedience required of him is delivery. Ibn Kathir brings the parallel: *"O Messenger! Proclaim which has been sent down to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His Message. Allah will protect you from mankind"* (5:67).

Then the other side of the transaction: *"and whosoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then verily, for him is the fire of Hell, he shall dwell therein forever."* Ibn Kathir: "I will convey unto you all the Messages of Allah, so whoever disobeys after that, then his reward will be the fire of Hell wherein he will abide forever" — meaning they will not be able to avoid it nor escape from it.

Notice the echo. In ayah 22 the Prophet ﷺ says of himself that if he disobeyed he would find "no place to escape to"; in ayah 23 the same helplessness is what awaits those who reject the message once it reaches them — they will not be able to avoid the Fire nor escape from it. His duty is to convey; theirs is to respond. Neither party can walk away from Allah.

## Ayah 24: who is really outnumbered

*"Till, when they see that which they are promised, then they will know who it is that is weaker concerning helpers and less important concerning numbers."* Ibn Kathir explains: until these idolaters from the jinn and humans see what has been promised to them on the Day of Judgement — then on that day, they will know whose helpers are weaker and fewer in number, theirs or the believers who worship Allah alone. And his conclusion: the idolaters have no helper at all, and they are fewer in number than the soldiers of Allah.

Set beside the third view of ayah 19 — the one Ibn Kathir preferred — the closing line reads as a reply. In that view the crowding was a display of numbers: humans and jinn crowded together over this matter in order to extinguish it, as Qatadah said, and Allah insisted upon helping it and making it victorious. Ayah 24 says the count is not finished. And the knowing comes with seeing: *when they see that which they are promised, then they will know*. What looked like a lone man surrounded will be seen as the party with helpers; the crowd will be seen as the party with none.

## Living it

- **Keep worship undivided.** Whatever else a mosque hosts, it belongs to Allah; Maʿārif's summary is that mosques must be kept clear of all false beliefs and vile deeds. And on the second reading of ayah 18, the ruling is not about buildings at all — prostration itself is His.
- **Watch where you turn when you need help.** Maʿārif's link is the sharpest practical point in the passage: calling on anyone other than Allah for help is as though you are prostrating to him.
- **Love the Prophet ﷺ the way he described himself.** Ayah 21 is his own disclaimer, in his own voice: no power over your harm, no power over your guidance — those things, Ibn Kathir says, are referred to Allah. Honouring him means responding to the message he was obligated to convey (ayah 23), not invoking him alongside Allah — which is the very thing ayah 18 forbids.
- **Don't let a crowd tell you what is true.** Whether the press around him was eager or hostile, the passage does not settle anything by weight of numbers, and ayah 24 promises that the numbers will look different when they are finally seen.
- **Take the servant's posture.** The passage's own picture of a worshipper is right there in ayah 19: the servant of Allah, standing, calling upon Him — with no claim to power and no refuge sought anywhere else.

passages.title: The Hour's timing and Allah's guarded unseen
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close Sūrat al-Jinn. They begin with a question the deniers pressed on the Prophet ﷺ — *when?* — and instead of answering with a date, they lift the reader to the far larger truth standing behind the date: the unseen belongs to Allah alone, and no creature attains any of His knowledge except what Allah allows him to have — delivered, when it is delivered, through a guarded channel to a chosen Messenger. Ayah 25 refuses the date. Ayah 26 explains why that refusal is not a flaw in prophethood. Ayah 27 carves out the single exception. Ayah 28 seals the whole thing by returning all knowledge — encompassing, and counted — to Allah.

## The demand behind ayah 25

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān tells us what provoked this ayah: the non-believers demanded that the Prophet ﷺ show them the exact time and date when the Resurrection would occur. In ayah 25 he is enjoined to say to them that it was not for him to say when the threatened punishment would come, **but come it must.**

Notice the shape of the reply. It opens with **قُلْ (qul), "Say"** — the answer is dictated to him, and the words he is given to speak are *"I know not."* Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to say to the people that he has no knowledge of when the Hour will be, and that he does not know whether its time is near or far.
