The ayah lays out two possibilities — *"I know not whether that which you are promised is near or whether my Lord will appoint for it a distant term"* — and places the Prophet ﷺ outside both. On **أَمَدًا (amadan)**, rendered "a distant term," Ibn Kathir comments: *meaning, a long period of time.* So it is not merely that he does not know the day; he does not even know the order of magnitude.

## What the Prophet ﷺ said when he was asked

Ibn Kathir observes that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about the time of the Hour and he would not respond. He records two occasions.

**The first:** when Jibrīl appeared to him in the form of a bedouin Arab, one of the questions he asked the Prophet ﷺ was, "O Muhammad! Tell me about the Hour?" So the Prophet ﷺ replied:

> **"The one questioned about it knows no more than the questioner."**

The one asked and the one asking are set on exactly the same footing.

**The second:** on another occasion a bedouin Arab called out to the Prophet ﷺ in a loud voice, "O Muhammad! When will be the Hour?" The Prophet ﷺ said:

> **"Woe unto you. Verily, it will occur so what have you prepared for it?"**

The man replied, "I have not prepared much for it of prayers and fasting, but I love Allah and His Messenger." The Prophet ﷺ then replied:

> **"Then you will be with whomever you love."**

Anas said, "The Muslims were not happier with anything like they were upon (hearing) this Hadith."

*(These reports appear in Ibn Kathir's commentary without a named collection attached, so they are related here as he relates them.)*

Look at what that second exchange does. The date is withheld; the *certainty* is not — *it will occur.* And once an event is certain but its timing is hidden, the only intelligent response left is readiness. The Prophet ﷺ takes a question about the calendar and hands it back as a question about the heart — and then, when the man confesses how thin his record of prayer and fasting is, he is not crushed but told that he will be with whomever he loves. Anas's remark tells you how that landed on the Muslims.

## Ibn Kathir's warning about a false report

Ibn Kathir uses this ayah to demolish a report that, he says, many of the ignorant people often circulate: that the Prophet ﷺ will not remain under the earth more than one thousand years — meaning the Hour would fall before that period. He calls it **a baseless lie**, and adds: *we have not seen it in any of the Books (of Hadith).*

The principle is worth carrying: **ayah 25 is a standing test for any claim that fixes, bounds, or narrows the date of the Hour.** If the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say "I know not," then no later calculation or circulating report is in a position to know.

## Ayah 26: why he does not know

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that ayah 26 is **the proof of the preceding ayah**. The Prophet ﷺ does not know whether the promised day is close or whether a longer time is appointed for it, *because Allah alone is the Knower of the Unseen.* That is His exclusive characteristic, and therefore He does not divulge His Unseen to anyone.

Two features of the Arabic carry the weight here, and Maʿārif draws both out:

**1. "The Unseen" — الْغَيْب with its definite article.** Grammarians call this *alif lām for istighrāq lil-jins* — "the article encompassing and indicating the entire genus" (Maʿārif states this from *Rūḥ*, with reference to Raḍī). In plain terms: the "the" here is not pointing at one particular hidden thing; it sweeps up **every kind and category of the unseen at once**. He is Omniscient — knowing every species of the Unseen and all genera of the Unseen.

**2. "His Unseen" — غَيْبِه.** In this *iḍāfah* (possessive) construction, the pronoun refers to Allah and **reinforces His predominance over the Unseen**. His knowledge comprehends and encompasses every species and every genus of His creation. Maʿārif calls this **a specialised attribute of Allah**.

Then comes the crucial qualification, in Maʿārif's own terms: **He does not divulge His Unseen to anyone indiscriminately, so that he may store and retrieve the secrets of the unknown world as and when he wishes.** That is the exact thing being denied — not that Allah ever informs anyone of anything hidden, but that any creature holds the unseen as a possession he can draw on at will.

Ibn Kathir sets the ayah beside another: *"And they will never compass any thing of His knowledge except that which He wills"* (2:255). His conclusion: Allah knows the unseen and the seen, and **no one of His creation can attain any of His knowledge except that which Allah allows him to have.**

## Ayah 27: the one door, and the guards on it

*"Except to a Messenger whom He has chosen…"* Ibn Kathir notes that this **includes the angelic Messenger and the human Messenger** — the angel who carries the revelation and the Prophet who receives it.

Then the ayah shows what the delivery route looks like: *"and then He makes a band of watching guards to march before him and behind him."* Ibn Kathir explains: **He particularly gives him additional guardian angels who protect him by the command of Allah, and they accompany him with that which is with him of Allah's revelation.** Maʿārif adds the purpose in one phrase: *so that devils may not tamper with the divine revelation.* The revelation is sent down through angels, and around those angels other angels are posted as sentinels.

**"Before him and behind him"** — the corridor is watched at both ends.

Ibn Kathir cites a striking detail from **Saʿīd bin Jubayr**, recorded by Ibn Jarīr and also by Ibn Abī Ḥātim: *"These are four guardians among the angels along with Jibrīl."* He notes that the same has been reported by **aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, as-Suddī and Yazīd bin Abī Ḥabīb.**

## The exception that does not cancel the rule

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān devotes its most careful passage to exactly what ayah 27 does and does not concede — because people have erred in both directions.

Maʿārif first states the purport of ayah 26: to affirm the totality of Allah's knowledge of the Unseen, so that He alone is fully aware of every particle of His creation, and to negate such total knowledge of the Unseen for anyone other than Allah. But an unintelligent person might then surmise that the Prophet ﷺ had no knowledge of the Unseen at all — so how could he be a Messenger? Allah reveals to a Messenger thousands of secrets of the Unseen; anyone to whom no revelation comes down cannot be a Prophet or a Messenger. And so the following ayah makes an exception.

The answer lies in the *kind* of exception being made. In Arabic grammar this is an **istithnā' munqaṭiʿ** — defined by Maʿārif as "the exceptive sentence in which the exception is severed from, or wholly different in kind from, the general description given before." So while the basic sentence in ayah 26 negates **total knowledge of the Unseen** in general terms for anyone besides Allah, the exceptive sentence in ayah 27 **does not affirm it.** What it affirms is something of a different order: specialised acquaintance with **some reports of the unseen events**, which the Qur'an frequently describes as **أَنبَاءِ الْغَيْب (anbā' al-ghayb)** — as in *"These are some reports from the unseen [events] which We reveal to you"* (11:49).

Maʿārif points out that the word **rasūl** in ayah 27 itself determines the type of knowledge granted: evidently, the knowledge of the sacred laws and injunctions in its totality, and of the unseen events according to the exigency of time. It is, in Maʿārif's phrase, **a specialised unseen knowledge which is essential and relevant to the proper functioning of a Prophetic office.**

From this Maʿārif marks off two errors:

**The error of excess.** Some, failing to grasp the distinction between "Knowledge of the Unseen" and "reports of the unseen events," attempt to prove *total* knowledge of the Unseen for the Prophets of Allah, especially for the Last Prophet ﷺ — believing him to be, like Allah, omniscient, having knowledge of every particle of the universe. Maʿārif states without hedging that this is **clearly shirk** — assigning to the Prophet ﷺ the status of Godhead, Allah forbid. Its illustration is homely and exact: if a person discloses a secret to a friend of his, of which no one else has that piece of knowledge, such a friend cannot be described as omniscient. Likewise, Allah has granted thousands of pieces of information of the unseen world through revelation to His Prophets ﷺ, but it is not true to say that they are omniscient.

**The error of deficiency.** Maʿārif is equally firm that when the ignorant are told the Prophet ﷺ is not omniscient, they understand it to imply that he ﷺ — Allah forbid — had no information about anything unseen at all. **No believer in the world ever holds such a belief, nor can he ever do so**, because if anyone did, the whole structure of *nubuwwah* (prophethood) and *risālah* (messengership) would come crumbling down.

Hold both together and the passage sits perfectly: the unseen in its totality belongs to Allah alone; a Messenger receives, through a guarded channel, precisely what the office he has been given requires.

## Ayah 28: "Till he knows"

The final ayah gives the purpose of all that guarding: *"Till he knows that they have conveyed the Messages of their Lord."* The Arabic **لِيَعْلَمَ (li-yaʿlama)** leaves its subject unstated, and the scholars differed over who is meant. Ibn Kathir lays the views out:

- **The Prophet ﷺ.** Ibn Kathir states that the pronoun 'he' in *"Till he knows"* refers to the Prophet ﷺ, and this is what Saʿīd bin Jubayr said — *"Till he knows"* means Muhammad ﷺ. ʿAbdur-Razzāq reported from Maʿmar, from Qatadah, expanding it: *"So that the Prophet of Allah would know that the Messengers had conveyed their Messages from Allah and that the angels have protected them and defended them."* The same has been reported by Saʿīd bin Abī ʿArūbah from Qatadah, and **Ibn Jarīr preferred this interpretation.**
- **The people.** Al-Baghawī said that **Yaʿqūb recited it as لِيُعْلَمَ (li-yuʿlama)** — a passive, "in order to be known" — meaning, *so that the people may know that the Messengers had conveyed the Message.*
- **Allah.** Ibn Kathir notes that it could also carry the meaning that the pronoun refers to Allah — an opinion mentioned by Ibn al-Jawzī in *Zād al-Masīr*. The meaning of this is that He protects His Messengers through His angels so that they will be able to convey His Messages, and He protects what He reveals to them of revelation, *so that He will know that they have indeed conveyed the Messages of their Lord.* Ibn Kathir supplies the parallels — *"And We made the Qiblah which you used to face, only that We know who followed the Messenger from those who would turn on their heels"* (2:143), and *"Verily, Allah knows those who believe, and that He knows the hypocrites"* (29:11) — and then, straight after those two examples, guards the point of creed: **from Allah's knowledge is that He knows all things before they occur, and this is something definite and certain.**

## "And He surrounds all that which is with them, and He keeps count of all things"

The closing clause answers any residual doubt the exception might have raised, and Ibn Kathir places it exactly there: *"Therefore, He says after this: And He surrounds all that which is with them, and He keeps count of all things."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the second half concrete. Rendering وَأَحْصَىٰ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ عَدَدًا as *"and has comprehensive knowledge of everything by numbers,"* it says: **Allah alone encompasses the perfect knowledge of everything and keeps a meticulous count of it.** He has the knowledge of the exact number of particles in the mountains; of the exact number of drops in all the oceans of the world; of the exact number of drops in every rain; He alone has the knowledge of the exact number of leaves on all the trees in the world. And Maʿārif states why this is placed here: **thus it is made clear that the totality of the knowledge of the Unseen is reserved exclusively for Allah, so that there should be no misunderstanding about the above 'exception' clause.** It notes that the question of the Unseen Knowledge is fully discussed under *"Say, 'No one in the heavens and the earth has the knowledge of the Unseen except Allah'"* (27:65).

## Living it

**Stop asking "when," start asking "what have I prepared?"** The passage models the redirection: an event that is certain but whose date is hidden calls for readiness, not arithmetic. And that second report is a mercy for anyone who looks at his own prayer and fasting and finds it thin — the man was not told his love counted for nothing because his deeds were few; he was told he would be with whomever he loves.

**Treat date-setting as answered in advance.** Ibn Kathir's dismissal of the "thousand years" report shows the method: measure the claim against ayah 25, and against the Prophet's ﷺ own words, *"The one questioned about it knows no more than the questioner."*

**Notice how the message was carried.** Ayah 27 is not an abstract point about angels. Revelation is sent down under guard — guardian angels who protect by the command of Allah and accompany the Messenger with what is with him of Allah's revelation. And on the reading Ibn Jarīr preferred, ayah 28 gives the Prophet ﷺ to know that the Messengers did convey their Messages from Allah, and that the angels protected them and defended them.

**Keep the unseen where Allah put it.** Between the man who claims a share in what belongs to Allah alone and the man who imagines revelation told the Prophet ﷺ nothing, ayah 26 and ayah 27 mark out the straight path: total knowledge of the Unseen is Allah's alone, and what a Messenger received of it was granted by Allah, guarded by Allah, and suited to the office Allah gave him.
